kapak.alt: No cochlea or nerve: the ABI

youtube.baslik: Auditory Brainstem Implant (ABI) | Lesson 248 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How can we reach hearing when there is no cochlea or no cochlear nerve? In this lesson we cover the logic of the auditory brainstem implant (ABI), neurofibromatosis type 2 and nontumor indications, electrode placement on the cochlear nucleus, initial activation and programming, expected outcomes and rehabilitation.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Colletti et al. (2009), Outcomes in nontumor adults fitted with the auditory brainstem implant: 10 years' experience, Otology and Neurotology; Sennaroglu et al. (2011), Auditory brainstem implantation in children and non-neurofibromatosis type 2 patients: a consensus statement, Otology and Neurotology; Wolfe, Cochlear Implants: Audiologic Management and Considerations for Implantable Hearing Devices; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: No cochlea or nerve: the ABI
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn about the implant that reaches the auditory pathway at the brainstem when a cochlear implant is not possible.
We will cover indications, electrode placement, programming and expected outcomes.
A cochlear implant needs two things to work: a cochlea to hold the electrodes and an auditory nerve to carry the stimulation.
If the cochlea never developed, or is too ossified for an electrode to be inserted, a cochlear implant cannot be used.
If the auditory nerve is absent or was cut during surgery, there is no nerve left for electrodes in the cochlea to stimulate.
The auditory brainstem implant, or ABI, bypasses both of these steps.
The electrodes are placed directly on the cochlear nucleus in the brainstem.
The cochlear nucleus is where the auditory nerve makes its first synapse in the brainstem.
From here, the signal follows the familiar central auditory pathway to reach the auditory cortex.

cumleler.yazi: In 1979, William House and William Hitselberger placed the first ABI, a single electrode, in a patient with neurofibromatosis type 2.
cumleler.ses: In nineteen seventy nine, William House and William Hitselberger placed the first ABI, a single electrode, in a patient with neurofibromatosis type 2.

cumleler: In the following years, systems with many electrodes on a flat, paddle-shaped carrier were developed.

cumleler.yazi: In the US, approval came in 2000 for patients with neurofibromatosis type 2 aged twelve years and older.
cumleler.ses: In the US, approval came in two thousand for patients with neurofibromatosis type 2 aged twelve years and older.

cumleler: In Europe, Colletti and colleagues began using the ABI in adults and children without tumors as well.

cumleler.yazi: In Türkiye, Sennaroglu and his team at Hacettepe University published extensive ABI experience in children with inner ear malformations.
cumleler.ses: In Türkiye, Sennarolu and his team at Hacettepe University published extensive ABI experience in children with inner ear malformations.

cumleler.yazi: In 2011, an international consensus statement was published on the ABI in children and in nontumor conditions.
cumleler.ses: In twenty eleven, an international consensus statement was published on the ABI in children and in nontumor conditions.

cumleler.yazi: The first and classic indication for the ABI is neurofibromatosis type 2, or NF2.
cumleler.ses: The first and classic indication for the ABI is neurofibromatosis type 2, or N F 2.

cumleler: In this genetic disease, bilateral vestibular schwannomas develop, arising from the vestibular nerve in the internal auditory canal.

cumleler.yazi: The current name of the disease is NF2-related schwannomatosis.
cumleler.ses: The current name of the disease is N F 2 related schwannomatosis.

cumleler: As the tumors grow or are removed surgically, the cochlear nerve is damaged and bilateral deafness may develop.
So the ABI is often placed in the same operation in which the tumor is removed.

cumleler.yazi: In selected NF2 patients whose cochlear nerve can be preserved, a cochlear implant may also be an option; the team decides.
cumleler.ses: In selected N F 2 patients whose cochlear nerve can be preserved, a cochlear implant may also be an option; the team decides.

cumleler: In children, the most common nontumor indication is cochlear nerve aplasia, where the cochlear nerve never developed.
When the nerve is very thin and the picture unclear, some centers first try a cochlear implant and consider an ABI if it is not enough.
In Michel aplasia, rudimentary otocyst and cochlear aplasia, seen in an earlier lesson, there is no cochlea; so the option is an ABI.
Complete ossification of the cochlea after meningitis, where no electrode can be inserted, is also an indication.
Avulsion of the cochlear nerve from a temporal bone fracture may also be considered for an ABI.
In all these conditions, diagnosis rests on magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, and CT, with audiological and electrophysiological findings.
The decision is made by an experienced team, after the expected outcomes have been explained to the family in detail.
Evaluation begins with detailed MRI and CT that show the state of the cochlea and the cochlear nerve.
Behavioral hearing tests and a suitable hearing aid trial show whether any residual hearing exists.
Electrophysiological tests give additional information on whether part of the auditory pathway can be stimulated.
The child's general development, additional disabilities and the family's ability to keep up with rehabilitation are also assessed.
All findings are discussed by a team of neurosurgeon, ear surgeon, audiologist, radiologist and speech and language therapist.
The family is told clearly that the ABI aims for a different and usually more limited outcome than a cochlear implant.
ABI surgery requires neurosurgical and ear surgery experience, and the two teams often work together.
The electrode carrier is advanced into the lateral recess of the fourth ventricle and seated on the surface of the cochlear nucleus.
The carrier is a small, flat paddle; depending on the manufacturer, it holds about twelve to twenty one electrodes.
Because the cochlear nucleus cannot be fully seen, anatomical landmarks are used to find the right position.
During surgery, the electrically evoked auditory brainstem response, or EABR, is recorded to see whether the auditory pathway is stimulated.
If needed, the carrier is moved in small steps until the best response is obtained.
The receiver-stimulator and external unit resemble those of a cochlear implant; the key difference is the electrode's position and shape.
Initial activation is often done in a hospital setting, with heart rhythm and vital signs monitored.
The reason is that stimulation in the brainstem can also affect other nearby neural structures.
Each electrode is stimulated one at a time, starting at a low level, and the person is asked whether there is any auditory sensation.
Electrodes that cause nonauditory sensations are switched off; some electrodes may produce no sensation at all.
The pitch order of electrodes that give auditory sensations is set one by one; unlike in a cochlear implant, this order is not regular.
The map is built from the electrodes that give auditory sensations, following their pitch order.
Because fewer electrodes can be used and levels vary, programming is a longer process that needs patience.
The most commonly reported nonauditory sensation is tingling somewhere in the body or in the face.
Dizziness or a feeling of swaying suggests that balance pathways are being stimulated.
Some people describe the image jittering or a movement in their eyes.
Sensations such as throat tightness or an urge to cough have also been reported.
These sensations usually stop when stimulation stops; they are resolved by switching off that electrode or changing the stimulation pattern.
In children who cannot talk, facial expression, eye movements and behavior are watched carefully to detect these sensations.
Outcomes with the ABI are usually more limited and more variable than with a cochlear implant.

cumleler.yazi: In most NF2 patients, the ABI provides awareness of environmental sounds and supports lipreading.
cumleler.ses: In most N F 2 patients, the ABI provides awareness of environmental sounds and supports lipreading.

cumleler.yazi: In the 2009 study by Colletti and colleagues, mean open-set speech recognition in NF2 patients was about ten percent.
cumleler.ses: In the two thousand nine study by Colletti and colleagues, mean open-set speech recognition in N F 2 patients was about ten percent.

cumleler: In the same study, the mean in adults without tumors was about fifty nine percent, and some could use the telephone.

cumleler.yazi: This difference is explained by the tumor and surgery in NF2 also being able to damage the cochlear nucleus.
cumleler.ses: This difference is explained by the tumor and surgery in N F 2 also being able to damage the cochlear nucleus.

cumleler: The values on the graph are the means of a single center; results may differ in other series.

cumleler.yazi: A small share of NF2 patients can also reach open-set speech understanding; so the outcome is judged separately for each person.
cumleler.ses: A small share of N F 2 patients can also reach open-set speech understanding; so the outcome is judged separately for each person.

cumleler: Most children with an ABI develop sound awareness and notice environmental sounds.
Some develop closed and open-set speech perception and spoken language; but progress is slower than in children with cochlear implants.
Early implantation and the absence of additional disabilities are usually linked to better outcomes.
Some children may need communication to continue with sign language or visual support.
Intensive, long-term auditory rehabilitation is an integral part of the ABI; the family is at the center of this process.
Before surgery, the family is told clearly that possible outcomes span a wide range.
Rehabilitation after an ABI starts from the lowest step of auditory skills, that is, detecting the presence of sounds.
In adults, listening is often practiced together with lipreading, because the ABI's most common benefit is making lipreading easier.
Then come work on discriminating and identifying sounds; these steps can take months and years.
Short, frequent and regular sessions are more effective than long but infrequent ones.
Goals are set for each person: hearing a knock at the door, the phone or one's own name are meaningful gains.
Improvement in lipreading skill is also measured, tracked and shared with the person.

sahneler.metin: At every visit, record in a table which electrodes give auditory and which give nonauditory sensations in the ABI user. Changes can occur over time; retest switched-off electrodes.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: at every visit, record which electrodes give auditory and which give nonauditory sensations for the ABI user.
The sensation an electrode gives can change over time; an electrode switched off earlier may later give an auditory sensation.
So retest switched-off electrodes at set intervals, starting from a low level.
Judge progress not only with speech tests but with goals that suit the person, such as sound awareness and help with lipreading.
The auditory brainstem implant bypasses the cochlea and auditory nerve and stimulates the cochlear nucleus in the brainstem directly.

cumleler.yazi: The classic indication is NF2; cochlear nerve aplasia, absent cochlea, severe ossification and trauma are nontumor indications.
cumleler.ses: The classic indication is N F 2; cochlear nerve aplasia, absent cochlea, severe ossification and trauma are nontumor indications.

cumleler: In programming, each electrode is tested one by one; those with nonauditory sensations are switched off, and pitch order is set per person.

cumleler.yazi: Outcomes are more limited and variable than with a cochlear implant; in nontumor patients they are usually better than in NF2.
cumleler.ses: Outcomes are more limited and variable than with a cochlear implant; in nontumor patients they are usually better than in N F 2.

sahneler.soru: What is the option if there is no cochlear nerve?
sahneler.aciklama: Without a nerve, stimulation goes directly to the _cochlear nucleus_.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in a child with cochlear nerve aplasia, which option could be considered instead of a cochlear implant?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: an auditory brainstem implant.
Without a cochlear nerve, electrodes in the cochlea have nothing to stimulate; the ABI stimulates the cochlear nucleus directly.
